posts.title: Make a small site easier for AI agents to use
posts.promise: Try Latch on a demo page and review the actions it exposes.
posts.whatItIs: Latch is an open-source WebMCP script that can expose a site's search, cart, contact or booking form actions as tools for an AI agent. A beginner's small experiment could install it on a test page and inspect the discovered actions; that student adaptation is hypothetical.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: a small website operator might pay for Latch's hosted dashboard if they want its opt-in agent activity analytics. The source lists a Pro plan at €19 per month per project; it does not establish customer demand.
loop: Add the provided script to a test site's page.
Let Latch inspect the page and register supported actions when WebMCP is available.
Use a test agent request such as searching for a sample item; the hypothetical output is a search result returned through the exposed search action.
Review the registered action and its result manually; a person must approve any purchase or form submission.
posts.evidence: Latch's site describes a one-line static script that exposes search, cart and contact or booking form actions as WebMCP tools, with no backend. It says the script is open source and offers an optional hosted analytics dashboard. The described demo includes a search and contact form.
posts.uncertainty: The source describes product capabilities but provides no independent usage or customer evidence. WebMCP availability varies; the site says Latch does nothing when it is unavailable. An exposed form or cart action can have consequences, so review inputs and results before submission or purchase. A beginner's test setup is a proposal, not an established customer workflow.
first24Hours: Create a disposable test page with a search field and contact form.
Add Latch's script and check which actions it detects in a supported browser.
Try a harmless sample search and manually inspect the result before enabling any send or purchase action.

ease.reason: The site says installation is one static script with no backend or build step, though a beginner still needs a test page and compatible browser.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: site operators might pay for the listed hosted dashboard, but the source gives no evidence of buyers or demand.

feasibility.reason: A test page can exercise the documented search action, while WebMCP availability and consequential form or cart actions need care.

autonomy.reason: The script can discover and register actions, but a person must review form submissions and purchases.

evidence.reason: The first-party site describes the working demo and product actions but supplies no independently documented real-use evidence.

posts.title: Try a local dictation and meeting-notes workflow
posts.promise: See how sideOS describes dictation, meeting summaries and review points.
posts.whatItIs: sideOS is a Mac assistant whose site describes on-device dictation and meeting transcription, plus summaries and action items. A beginner could try a short, non-sensitive recording and check the transcript and summary; this test adaptation is hypothetical.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: an individual Mac user may pay for the app's listed lifetime licence. The source lists a one-time price of $89.90 but does not establish buyer demand or sales.
loop: Start dictation or manually choose to record a meeting; the site says recording is offered and does not start on its own.
For the hypothetical test, use a short sample recording with consent from everyone involved.
Let the app transcribe the audio on the Mac and draft a summary and action items.
A person checks names, wording and action items against the recording before sharing or creating reminders.
Choose whether to keep or delete the audio using the app's retention setting.
posts.evidence: The product site describes dictation using macOS speech engines and says meeting transcription runs on-device. It says a call window prompts the user to record, then the app produces a transcript, summary and actions; action items can become reminders. It lists a $89.90 one-time licence.
posts.uncertainty: These are first-party product claims; the attached page does not establish accuracy or independent customer use. A person should obtain recording consent, verify names and decisions, and approve any reminder or shared summary. The short sample workflow is a hypothetical test, and performance may depend on macOS and the audio.
first24Hours: Check that you have a compatible Mac and choose a non-sensitive short audio sample.
If recording other people, ask for their consent before starting; otherwise use your own sample speech.
Compare the generated transcript and summary with the audio, correcting errors before using any action items.

ease.reason: The source describes a simple dictation gesture and meeting prompt, but the experiment requires a compatible Mac and careful handling of recordings.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: Mac users might buy the listed lifetime licence, but the source supplies no customer or sales evidence.

feasibility.reason: A short recording can demonstrate the described transcription and summary loop, though Mac access, consent and transcript review are required.

autonomy.reason: Transcription and drafting are automated, while recording is user-started and a person must verify the summary and actions.

evidence.reason: The first-party site provides detailed feature descriptions and demonstrations, but no independent evidence of actual customer use.

refusals.reason: The attached repository page identifies Shotstash as a self-hosted media cloud for creators and shows repository metadata, but provides no usable product workflow or demonstration evidence from which to write a beginner post without inventing capabilities.
